documents.title: Syllabus Minimum Requirements Policy (Artificial Intelligence (AI) Usage section)
documents.summary: A curriculum-management policy listing what every course syllabus must contain. Its only AI content is one line requiring an AI usage policy in each syllabus while leaving permitted or prohibited use to the instructor.
documents.stance_why: The AI section says every syllabus needs an AI usage policy but that 'Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor.' It sets no university-wide permit or ban and hands the decision to instructors, so the stance is delegates.

units.why: The policy requires every syllabus to carry an AI policy ('must include'), which is the 'require an AI statement' type; it binds instructors who write syllabi, at course design time.
units.anchor: All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy

units.why: This sentence leaves the permit-or-prohibit decision to the instructor ('remains at the discretion of the instructor'), so it is P04, not a default rule such as P01 or P02.
units.anchor: remains at the discretion of the instructor

documents.unit: Division of Academic Affairs (Senior Vice Provost)
documents.title: University Guidance on the Use of Generative AI in Teaching and Learning (memo to faculty)
documents.summary: A September 2025 memo from the Senior Vice Provost to faculty introducing university guidance on generative AI and a syllabus statement. It strongly encourages, but does not yet require, instructors to adopt both and lists workshops and consultations.
documents.stance_why: The memo says instructors are 'strongly encouraged' to follow the guidance and add a GenAI syllabus statement 'tailoring it with details of the specific approach to the use of GenAI in the course.' It states no rule on student AI use itself and leaves the approach to each course, so delegates.

units.why: The memo names the values the guidance reflects ('human cognition and creativity, academic integrity, and inclusive excellence'), an institution-level statement of principles, so P56.
units.anchor: OSU's shared commitments to human cognition and creativity, academic integrity, and inclusive excellence

units.why: The guidance is said to 'support faculty autonomy and intellectual freedom', which places course decisions with faculty; P04 fits better than P56 because the point is who decides.
units.anchor: support faculty autonomy and intellectual freedom

units.why: The guidance aims to 'protect the privacy and security of individual and institutional data', a privacy principle, so P50.
units.anchor: protect the privacy and security of individual and institutional data

units.why: Instructors are 'strongly encouraged' to follow the guidance and add the GenAI syllabus statement, tailored to the course. This recommends putting an AI statement in the syllabus, so P09 with should.
units.anchor: Add the GenAI syllabus statement to their syllabi
units.policy: Instructors are strongly encouraged to add the GenAI syllabus statement to their syllabi, tailoring it with details of the specific approach to the use of GenAI in the course.
units.fit_note: Encouraged this term, not yet required; the statement is to be tailored to the course.

units.why: The memo says the statement will 'eventually become a syllabus requirement' after Faculty Senate vetting. It is about the policy changing over time, so P54; P09 does not fit because nothing is required yet.
units.anchor: a GenAI statement will eventually become a syllabus requirement
units.fit_note: Also announces an expected future syllabus requirement, not only that the policy is provisional.

units.why: The memo points faculty to a workshop, drop-in hours and consultations to help tailor a statement, which is support for faculty learning, P63.
units.anchor: Register for the upcoming workshop
units.policy: Faculty can attend a workshop and drop-in hours, review CTL and Ecampus AI resources, or schedule a CTL or Ecampus consultation to help tailor their syllabus statement.

documents.title: Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning
tiers: Minor Uses Permitted for AI Tools
AI Use Encouraged and Fully Permitted
Specific Expectations and Notes for AI Use
documents.summary: The Center for Teaching and Learning's guidance for instructors on AI in teaching: definitions, which AI tools to use with student work, rules for instructors' own AI use, and a syllabus-statement template with five icon tiers from 'Do Not Use' to 'Fully Permitted'. Instructors pick the tier and add detail.
documents.stance_why: The page offers a template with five icon tiers (from 'Do Not Use' to 'AI Use Encouraged and Fully Permitted') and says 'Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor.' Because it supplies tiers and leaves the choice to instructors, the stance is delegates.

units.why: The guidance says AI integration 'must reflect our shared commitments to human cognition and creativity, academic integrity, and inclusive excellence', an institution-level principle statement, so P56.
units.anchor: must reflect our shared commitments to human cognition and creativity, academic integrity

units.why: The guidance 'supports faculty autonomy and intellectual freedom' in designing AI use in courses, which places the decision with faculty (P04).
units.anchor: supports faculty autonomy and intellectual freedom

units.why: Defines AI as a set of 'advanced digital technologies' that do complex tasks; a definition that sets the scope of the guidance, so P61.
units.anchor: a broad set of advanced digital technologies

units.why: Defines generative AI and says it 'includes both standalone offerings, such as ChatGPT, and offerings that are embedded in other software such as Microsoft 365's Copilot', fixing the scope (P61) and covering embedded AI.
units.anchor: offerings that are embedded in other software such as Microsoft 365's Copilot
units.fit_note: Also states that embedded AI (Copilot) counts as GenAI, which touches P07.

units.why: Employees are told 'You are welcome to use AI tools' with a preference for approved ones; a general permission for staff and instructors, so P02, aimed at instructors.
units.anchor: You are welcome to use AI tools

units.why: Instructors and staff 'are encouraged' to use OSU's approved AI tools whenever possible because they give security and data protection; preferring vetted tools is P50.
units.anchor: instructors and staff are encouraged to utilize
units.policy: Instructors and staff are encouraged to use OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools whenever possible.

units.why: OSU employees 'may explore other AI tools, provided no confidential, sensitive, or student information' is included, a data-protection limit on non-approved tools (P50).
units.anchor: OSU employees may explore other AI tools, provided no confidential, sensitive, or student information

units.why: UIT 'maintains the list' of approved tools, which tells readers who governs which tools count as approved; this is vetted-tool governance (P50).
units.anchor: is the authority on and maintains the list
units.policy: University Information and Technology (UIT) is the authority on and maintains the list of OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools.

units.why: Instructors 'may not input student work into any AI tools or applications that are not approved by OSU', a ban on putting student work in non-approved tools to protect privacy (P50).
units.anchor: may not input student work into any AI tools or applications that are not approved

units.why: The page restates that every syllabus 'must include an AI usage policy', a syllabus-statement requirement (P09).
units.anchor: All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy

units.why: 'Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor' puts the rule per instructor (P04).
units.anchor: remains at the discretion of the instructor

units.why: Instructors are 'strongly encouraged to identify in a syllabus statement' whether AI will make materials or review student work, i.e. tell students about instructor AI use (P47).
units.anchor: strongly encouraged to identify in a syllabus statement

units.why: 'Instructors may use AI to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, assignments, or assessments' states what instructors may use AI for in teaching work (P59).
units.anchor: Instructors may use AI to create, augment, or refine instructional materials

units.why: Instructors who use AI substantially for materials 'are strongly encouraged to disclose in a syllabus statement'. The topic is AI-made materials, so P48 rather than P47.
units.anchor: strongly encouraged to disclose in a syllabus statement their AI usage

units.why: Instructors are 'required to review instructional materials created by AI', a review duty for AI-made materials (P48).
units.anchor: required to review instructional materials created by AI

units.why: Instructors 'may direct students to use AI applications and tools as part of their learning', letting the instructor decide to assign AI use; P04 is closest, since it is a per-activity choice.
units.anchor: may direct students to use AI applications and tools as part of their learning
units.fit_note: Says instructors may assign AI use; P04 captures the instructor's choice but not that assigning AI is explicitly allowed.

units.why: Non-approved tools 'may be required' if students need not enter 'their own creative works, sensitive data, or personally identifiable information'; a data-protection condition on assigned tools (P50).
units.anchor: as long as the assigned activities do not require a student to enter their own

units.why: Instructors 'must use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools' when students must enter their own works or sensitive data: a vetted-tool rule to protect student data (P50).
units.anchor: tools if the student is required to enter their own creative works
units.policy: Instructors must use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools if the student is required to enter their own creative works, sensitive data, or personally identifiable information into the AI tool.

units.why: Instructors 'are encouraged to use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools as part of the requirements for course activities', pushing a sanctioned tool into assignments (P17).
units.anchor: encouraged to use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools as part of the requirements

units.why: Instructors 'may use' approved tools for an 'initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials against a rubric': what instructors may use AI for in teaching work (P59).
units.anchor: to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials
units.policy: Instructors may use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials against a rubric.

units.why: 'Instructors are ultimately responsible for assigning grades based on their human evaluation of student work' says humans give grades (P46).
units.anchor: instructors are ultimately responsible for assigning grades based on their human evaluation of student work

units.why: Instructors are 'strongly encouraged to disclose to students' if approved AI tools will review or score work: disclosing instructor AI use in grading (P47).
units.anchor: strongly encouraged to disclose to students in their syllabus statement

units.why: Instructors are 'required to review feedback for students created by AI': a review duty on AI-drafted feedback. It is not about disclosure or final grades, so P59 with a fit note.
units.anchor: required to review feedback for students created by AI
units.fit_note: States a duty to review AI-drafted feedback before it reaches students; P59 lists uses, not review duties.

units.why: The syllabus template says AI 'should only be used for coursework in ways that adhere to individual instructor guidelines'. The rule is set per instructor (P04).
units.anchor: should only be used for coursework in ways that adhere to individual instructor guidelines

units.why: The template says 'When AI use is permitted, care must be taken to use these tools responsibly.' This is a general duty of responsible use that none of the listed types states specifically.
units.anchor: care must be taken to use these tools responsibly
units.uncovered_note: General duty to use permitted AI responsibly, with no concrete content.

units.why: 'students are responsible for reviewing individual course policies and understanding appropriate use in each course' tells students that rules differ by course, which is P11.
units.anchor: students are responsible for reviewing individual course policies

units.why: Students are told 'Please contact the instructor if you have questions about specific AI tools': ask before using when unsure (P10).
units.anchor: Please contact the instructor if you have questions about specific AI tools

units.why: The template tells instructors to 'Choose one of the options below' of icon-labelled categories, which sets named tiers of AI use (P05).
units.anchor: Choose one of the options below to copy/paste here
units.policy: Instructors choose one of the icon-labelled tier options (Do Not Use, Minor Uses Permitted, AI Tools Integrated by Assignment, AI Use Encouraged and Fully Permitted, Specific Expectations) for their syllabus statement.

units.why: The 'Do Not Use' tier says AI use to 'generate or edit any portion of the substance of your work is not permitted unless explicitly noted'. This is a default ban with assignment-level exceptions (P01).
units.anchor: is not permitted unless explicitly noted in the assignment instructions
units.policy: In the Do Not Use tier, the use of any AI tools to generate or edit any portion of the substance of your work is not permitted unless explicitly noted in the assignment instructions.

units.why: The same tier accepts AI embedded in everyday tools such as Word grammar check but says 'you are not allowed to use AI for your coursework beyond these limited non-substantive supports'. This covers embedded AI, so P07.
units.anchor: you are not allowed to use AI for your coursework beyond these limited non-substantive supports
units.fit_note: Carves out limited non-substantive AI built into Word, PowerPoint and search engines while banning other AI use.

units.why: The 'Minor Uses' tier says 'you must be the sole author of all work', a rule that submitted work is the student's own (P29).
units.anchor: you must be the sole author of all work

units.why: The optional line says language generated by an AI tool must be attributed 'by putting that language in quotation marks and adding a citation': a disclosure and citation duty (P24).
units.anchor: you must attribute that use by putting that language in quotation marks and adding a

units.why: The 'Integrated by Assignment' tier says 'Review individual assignments to determine permissible uses', so the rule is set per assignment (P04).
units.anchor: Review individual assignments to determine permissible uses

units.why: In that tier students should 'be able to demonstrate how you contributed to the work you submit', an ownership and accountability rule (P29).
units.anchor: you should be able to demonstrate how you contributed to the work you submit

units.why: The tier's example requires students to 'keep drafts of assignments and generative AI logs that demonstrate how you used AI', which is keeping logs and drafts (P26).
units.anchor: you are required to keep drafts of assignments and generative AI logs

units.why: The top tier says 'you are encouraged to experiment with AI and AI tools': an encouraging default (P02).
units.anchor: you are encouraged to experiment with AI and AI tools

units.why: Even in the open tier 'You should not enter creative works, sensitive data, or personally identifiable information into AI tools': a data-protection limit (P50).
units.anchor: You should not enter creative works, sensitive data, or personally identifiable information into AI tools

units.why: Instructors should 'use both the visual indicator and a detailed description' since 'Using the visual indicator alone is not fully accessible'. This instructs how to communicate the AI policy, so P09, with an accessibility note.
units.anchor: use both the visual indicator and a detailed description of the specific application of this
units.fit_note: Adds that icons alone are not accessible and that detail must also appear in assignment language.

units.why: Instructors should list 'Examples of specific tasks for which students may be allowed to use AI' such as generating ideas, self-quizzing, outlining. This is guidance on spelling out permitted uses in the syllabus, so P09.
units.anchor: Examples of specific tasks for which students may be allowed to use AI
units.policy: Instructors should include examples of specific tasks for which students may be allowed to use AI: generate ideas, polish or edit drafted text, create an outline of an essay, modify or design presentation slides, review content, self-quizzing, or other studying purposes.
units.fit_note: The content lists permitted uses (ideas, editing, outlining, self-quizzing); P09 captures only the duty to specify.

units.why: The guidance lists tasks the syllabus may bar, including 'for any purpose while taking a quiz or test'. This is a ban on AI in assessments, shown as a syllabus example (P22).
units.anchor: for any purpose while taking a quiz or test
units.policy: Instructors may state that students may not use AI for any purpose while taking a quiz or test.

units.why: The same list names 'generate content that is directly used in an assignment (such as code, text, images, or other media)' as a task that may be barred, i.e. AI producing submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: generate content that is directly used in an assignment (such as code, text, images, or
units.policy: Instructors may state that students may not use AI to generate content that is directly used in an assignment (such as code, text, images, or other media), solve problems from assignments, write a first draft of a paper or essay, write all or part of a discussion post or analyze data.

units.why: Instructors should state which tools they 'do or do not want students to use', a tool-specific element of the syllabus statement (P09).
units.anchor: AI tools that you do or do not want students to use

units.why: Instructors should say 'why you have selected policy (e.g., to support skill development...)', giving students the reasons behind the rule (P66).
units.anchor: Briefly, why you have selected policy

units.why: 'Revisit the statement each term' asks instructors to review their AI statement regularly (P54).
units.anchor: Revisit the statement each term

units.why: Instructors are pointed to CTL and Ecampus for guidance and examples, which is faculty support (P63).
units.anchor: The Center for Teaching and Learning and Ecampus offer additional guidance

documents.title: CTL Guidance for Syllabus Statements about AI Use
documents.summary: A CTL page of advice for writing a course AI syllabus statement: it points to the university categories and template, recommends trying Copilot first, advises against detectors, and urges instructors to explain the policy to students. It sets no stance on student AI use itself.
documents.stance_why: The page quotes the rule that 'Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor' and then advises how instructors might draft their own statement ('You are encouraged to modify the language to fit your approach'). It sets no rule for students, so delegates.

units.why: The page says AI is 'embedded in many writing tools (for example, Grammarly, online translators, and Googe Docs autocomplete)', context about embedded AI that bears on policy scope (P07).
units.anchor: AI is ubiquitous and embedded in many writing tools

units.why: 'Completely prohibiting the use of AI is increasingly impractical, and AI use is not accurately detectable' is an argument against blanket bans that no listed type captures.
units.anchor: Completely prohibiting the use of AI is increasingly impractical
units.uncovered_note: States that a complete ban on AI is impractical, as a reason for instructors to avoid blanket prohibition.

units.why: Instructors are told 'we do not recommend mentioning them [detectors] in syllabus statements or using them as a basis for student conduct cases', so AI detectors are not to be relied on (P39).
units.anchor: we do not recommend mentioning them in syllabus statements or using them as a basis

units.why: The page quotes the rule that 'All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy', a syllabus-statement requirement (P09).
units.anchor: must include an AI usage policy that communicates expectations

units.why: It also quotes 'Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor', leaving the rule per instructor (P04).
units.anchor: remains at the discretion of the instructor

units.why: Every syllabus must 'include a link to the Student Conduct Expectations regardless of the particular course AI policy', tying AI rules to the conduct process. No exact type fits; P09 is nearest since it is a syllabus content rule.
units.anchor: required to include a link to the Student Conduct Expectations
units.fit_note: Requires a conduct-code link in every syllabus, not an AI statement itself.

units.why: CTL 'encourages you to communicate with your students at the start of the term to make clear the relationship between the course AI policy and the Code of Student Conduct', i.e. explain the rules to students (P66).
units.anchor: encourages you to communicate with your students at the start of the term

units.why: Instructors are told to 'Try out Microsoft Copilot' and other tools to inform their policy, which is faculty learning (P63).
units.anchor: Try out Microsoft Copilot
units.policy: Instructors should try out Microsoft Copilot, OSU's recommended and approved AI tool, and other free AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude, so their experience informs their course policy.

units.why: 'Discuss AI teaching approaches and unit-wide AI policies with your colleagues and unit leaders' encourages faculty to build understanding together (P63).
units.anchor: Discuss AI teaching approaches and unit-wide AI policies with your colleagues and unit leaders

units.why: 'OSU AI guidance identifies several categories of course AI policies, ranging from no AI use to fully accepted and encouraged AI use' describes named tiers of use (P05).
units.anchor: several categories of course AI policies, ranging from no AI use to fully accepted and

units.why: 'You are encouraged to modify the language ... and to describe your reasons for the policy you adopt' asks instructors to give reasons (P66).
units.anchor: to describe your reasons for the policy you adopt

units.why: Instructors are 'strongly encouraged to disclose your own AI use on your syllabus', which 'models transparency': disclosure of instructor AI use (P47).
units.anchor: strongly encouraged to disclose your own AI use on your syllabus

units.why: 'be sure assignment and assessment directions are in alignment with your course policy' asks for consistency between the syllabus and assignments; nearest is P09, as a duty to state the policy at assignment level.
units.anchor: assignment and assessment directions are in alignment with your course policy
units.fit_note: Asks that assignment directions match the course AI policy, not only that a syllabus statement exist.

units.why: 'Conversations with your students at the beginning of the term about your AI policy and the reasoning behind it' are recommended so the rules are discussed (P66).
units.anchor: Conversations with your students at the beginning of the term about your AI policy

units.why: The page offers a ten-minute PowerPoint and 'blanket permission to OSU faculty who would like to adapt it' to introduce students to AI and the course policy, an example of explaining rules to students (P66).
units.anchor: blanket permission to OSU faculty who would like to adapt it for their use
units.policy: A faculty member's brief PowerPoint introducing students to generative AI, AI literacy and her course AI policy is available for OSU faculty to adapt.

units.why: 'As the term progresses, check on your students concerning your AI policy and their use of AI' asks for ongoing follow-up during the course (P66).
units.anchor: check on your students concerning your AI policy and their use of AI
units.fit_note: Concerns follow-up check-ins during the term rather than explaining the rules at the start.

units.why: CTL 'supports an ethic of transparency around the use of generative AI in teaching and learning', a principle statement that sets the purpose of the guidance (P56).
units.anchor: supports an ethic of transparency around the use of generative AI

documents.title: Generative AI Guidelines for Ecampus Course Development
documents.summary: Ecampus guidelines for how faculty and staff may use generative AI when developing online courses. They encourage AI use that streamlines development but require careful consideration of risky uses, approved tools, full faculty review, labeling and a syllabus acknowledgment.
documents.stance_why: The guideline says 'Ecampus encourages AI use in ways that advance innovation and streamline course development, while upholding the authenticity and quality of the student learning experience', then attaches conditions (review, labeling, approved tools, no full AI-produced critical content). Allowed with conditions, so permit; it governs course development, not student work.

units.why: Ecampus 'encourages AI use in ways that advance innovation and streamline course development', a statement of what staff and faculty may use AI for in course work (P59), phrased as encouragement.
units.anchor: encourages AI use in ways that advance innovation and streamline course development

units.why: Ecampus 'will adhere to OSU's Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning' alongside its own rules, which makes the university guidance binding on this work (P77).
units.anchor: Ecampus will adhere to OSU’s Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning

units.why: Staff and faculty 'should carefully consider' routine or experimental AI uses that significantly affect authorship, instructor presence or student interaction. This guides what staff may use AI for in teaching work (P59).
units.anchor: carefully consider the use of generative AI, either routine or experimental, that significantly affects authorship

units.why: The list flags 'generating or simulating the instructor's voice, image, or persona in learning content' for careful consideration, a specific limit on instructor AI use in teaching work (P59).
units.anchor: generating or simulating the instructor’s voice, image, or persona in learning content

units.why: The list flags 'creating course chat bots' for careful consideration, which concerns building a course AI tool and fits P59 (instructor and staff uses) more than P17 (a sanctioned tool for students).
units.anchor: creating course chat bots
units.policy: Ecampus staff and faculty partners should carefully consider creating course chat bots.

units.why: The list flags 'tools that promote AI-assisted grading (i.e. using auto-grading functionality in Perusall or Gradescope)' because of teaching quality. It concerns AI in grading; P46 (humans assign grades) does not say this, so P59.
units.anchor: using tools that promote AI-assisted grading
units.policy: Ecampus staff and faculty partners should carefully consider using tools that promote AI-assisted grading, such as the auto-grading functionality in Perusall or Gradescope, because of the potential impact on teaching quality and regular-and-substantive interaction requirements.
units.fit_note: Concerns AI-assisted grading tools and regular-and-substantive interaction rules, not a ban on AI grading.

units.why: Ecampus staff 'will discuss implications of using generative AI with the faculty developer', a consultation step that supports faculty in thinking through AI use (P63).
units.anchor: will discuss implications of using generative AI with the faculty developer

units.why: Voice automation should come with 'being transparent when it's employed', telling learners about instructor-side AI use (P47).
units.anchor: being transparent when it’s employed

units.why: 'Ecampus multimedia staff will not use AI tools to produce critical course content in full' is a firm limit on staff AI use in course materials (P59).
units.anchor: Ecampus multimedia staff will not use AI tools to produce critical course content in full

units.why: Staff 'will use only OSU's approved Gen AI tools' with faculty-created materials, a vetted-tool rule that protects faculty content (P50).
units.anchor: will use only OSU’s approved Gen AI tools when working with faculty-created instructional materials

units.why: Non-approved tools 'require instructor permission', adding a consent condition to the vetted-tool rule (P50).
units.anchor: Use of non-OSU approved AI tools requires instructor permission
units.fit_note: Adds that instructor permission can allow non-approved tools.

units.why: AI-generated course content 'will require full review by the faculty developer, who will be accountable for its accuracy', a review duty for AI-made materials (P48).
units.anchor: will require full review by the faculty developer, who will be accountable for its accuracy

units.why: 'Learning objects created with generative AI will be labeled clearly': a labeling duty for AI-made materials (P48).
units.anchor: Learning objects created with generative AI will be labeled clearly

units.why: Courses that use AI substantially 'will acknowledge this with a syllabus statement at minimum', a disclosure to students about AI-made materials (P48).
units.anchor: will acknowledge this with a syllabus statement at minimum

units.why: Future AI uses 'should align with the seven principles outlined in our Ecampus AI ethics statement and may require department approval', which points to a framework of principles (P56).
units.anchor: should align with the seven principles outlined in our Ecampus AI ethics statement

documents.unit: College of Engineering (Academic Integrity Resources for Faculty)
documents.title: AI Chatbot Policy Example
documents.summary: A College of Engineering example course policy that allows AI chatbots for finding errors, verifying algorithms, small code snippets and small pieces of written reports, while forbidding chatbots writing the software or documents. It explains each limit by learning and career reasons.
documents.stance_why: The text repeats 'You ARE allowed to use' chatbots for errors, verification, small snippets and creative elements, with 'You ARE NOT allowed to use AI chatbots to simply write your software for you, or write your documents for you.' AI is allowed with conditions, so permit.

units.why: The policy lets students use chatbots 'as you would a library resource', treating AI like an outside source (P45).
units.anchor: AI chatbots as you would a library resource

units.why: Students may use ChatGPT 'to find solutions for errors the same way you would use Stackoverflow', which is help with errors and debugging (P13).
units.anchor: use ChatGPT to find solutions for errors the same way you would use Stackoverflow

units.why: Students may use chatbots 'to understand and improve software you are developing', using AI to understand rather than to write (P12).
units.anchor: to understand and improve software you are developing

units.why: 'You ARE allowed to use AI chatbots to verify algorithms': a self-check of student-developed work (P14).
units.anchor: allowed to use AI chatbots to verify algorithms
units.fit_note: Verification of algorithms the student already developed, not practice problems or study aids.

units.why: 'You will learn more if you develop your algorithms yourself' says doing the work builds skill and asking AI to generate it is a shortcut (P41).
units.anchor: You will learn more if you develop your algorithms yourself

units.why: 'In your career, there are guaranteed to be problems for which AI cannot propose algorithms or solutions' gives a career reason to build critical thinking; closest is P41 (skill-building), though it is career-framed.
units.anchor: there are guaranteed to be problems for which AI cannot propose algorithms or solutions
units.fit_note: Frames the loss of critical thinking skill as a career risk with employers.

units.why: Students 'ARE allowed to use AI chatbots for small snippets of code', a conditional permission for AI-generated code (P16).
units.anchor: allowed to use AI chatbots for small snippets of code

units.why: Snippets from any source must not 'introduce software license restrictions or the possibility of copyright, trademark, trade secret' problems, a licensing concern (P52).
units.anchor: do not introduce software license restrictions or the possibility of copyright, trademark, trade secret

units.why: 'It is wiser and safer to adapt the principles demonstrated in those snippets to your own code... rather than simply pasting something into your code verbatim' is advice against pasting; nearest is P23, which covers not copy-pasting from AI.
units.anchor: adapt the principles demonstrated in those snippets to your own code
units.policy: It is wiser and safer to adapt the principles demonstrated in those snippets to your own code, and to the context in which the snippets need to run, rather than simply pasting something into your code verbatim.
units.fit_note: Framed as a professional-safety recommendation, not a strict separation of AI and work.

units.why: Students may use chatbots for 'written reports or other creative elements (not whole blocks or reports)', a separate prose rule from the code one (P18).
units.anchor: generating written reports or other creative elements (not whole blocks or reports)

units.why: 'You should never blindly submit something based on AI chatbots without using critical thinking and good judgment' tells students to verify AI output (P31).
units.anchor: never blindly submit something based on AI chatbots without using critical thinking and good judgment

units.why: 'You won't get proper credit for work based on incorrect or invalid output' warns of a grade effect from wrong AI output; it reinforces P31 rather than naming a penalty for misconduct (P37).
units.anchor: You won't get proper credit for work based on incorrect or invalid output

units.why: Students should 'be thoughtful and judicious about how much you use these or any tools as a replacement for your work', i.e. stay the main problem solver (P32).
units.anchor: be thoughtful and judicious about how much you use these or any tools as a

units.why: 'send me an email explaining your planned use' tells unsure students to ask the instructor first (P10).
units.anchor: send me an email explaining your planned use

units.why: 'ARE NOT allowed to use AI chatbots to simply write your software for you, or write your documents' bans AI producing the submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: use AI chatbots to simply write your software for you, or write your documents

units.why: Students who submit generated responses 'will be subject to an Academic Integrity violation': AI misuse handled as misconduct (P36).

documents.unit: School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS)
documents.title: Guidance on Drafting AI Use Policies
documents.summary: The EECS school's June 2026 common floor for AI policies: definitions, rules for faculty use, a default for students when a syllabus is silent, disclosure and attribution, a research section, syllabus expectations, academic-integrity and detection rules, and appendices with nine use categories and research disclosure tiers. Individual instructors set the course rules.
documents.stance_why: The guidance says 'While individual faculty will set course-specific rules, this document provides the common floor and vocabulary' and supplies nine use categories (Appendix A) that 'Course policies will specify.' It sets a fallback and some bans but leaves each course to choose, so delegates.

units.why: 'This statement establishes shared expectations for AI use across EECS courses' sets the purpose and scope of a unit-wide framework (P56).
units.anchor: establishes shared expectations for AI use across EECS courses

units.why: 'While individual faculty will set course-specific rules, this document provides the common floor and vocabulary' leaves the course rule to each instructor (P04).
units.anchor: individual faculty will set course-specific rules

units.why: 'Where those documents conflict with this one, OSU policy governs' says university policy outranks this one (P77).
units.anchor: Where those documents conflict with this one, OSU policy governs

units.why: 'a college-wide AI policy for the College of Engineering is in development; this document will be updated' says the policy is provisional (P54).
units.anchor: this document will be updated to align with it when finalized

units.why: Defines GenAI as built on foundation models and to include 'standalone tools, agentic systems, multi-modal pipelines, and automated workflows', setting what the policy covers (P61), including agents.
units.anchor: standalone tools, agentic systems, multi-modal pipelines, and automated workflows

units.why: 'Faculty may use GenAI to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, assignments, or assessments' is a permitted instructor use (P59).
units.anchor: Faculty may use GenAI to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, assignments, or assessments

units.why: Faculty 'are required to review instructional materials created by GenAI', a review duty for AI-made materials (P48).
units.anchor: required to review instructional materials created by GenAI

units.why: Faculty who use AI substantially are 'strongly encouraged to disclose in a syllabus statement', with routine grammar help exempt: disclosure for AI-made materials (P48).
units.anchor: strongly encouraged to disclose in a syllabus statement their AI usage
units.fit_note: Also exempts routine grammar assistance, search and autocomplete from disclosure.

units.why: Faculty 'may use OSU Recommended and Approved GenAI tools to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials': a permitted instructor use (P59).
units.anchor: to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials
units.policy: Faculty may use OSU Recommended and Approved GenAI tools to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials against a rubric.

units.why: 'Grades must reflect the faculty member's own evaluation of student work' means humans decide grades (P46).
units.anchor: Grades must reflect the faculty member's own evaluation of student work

units.why: 'Faculty must disclose in their syllabus statement when GenAI tools will be used in any part of the grading or feedback process' requires telling students about instructor AI use (P47).
units.anchor: Faculty must disclose in their syllabus statement when GenAI tools will be used

units.why: 'Only OSU Recommended and Approved tools may be used when assessing student work' is a vetted-tool rule for protecting student records (P50).
units.anchor: Only OSU Recommended and Approved tools may be used when assessing student work

units.why: 'Faculty must explain their GenAI use policy in their course' makes faculty state their AI rules (P09).
units.anchor: Faculty must explain their GenAI use policy in their course

units.why: 'Students may not recognize that AI-assisted features in common development tools constitute GenAI use' warns that embedded features count (P07).
units.anchor: AI-assisted features in common development tools constitute GenAI use under this policy

units.why: 'Students may use AI tools when course policies explicitly permit it' makes permission the condition for use, i.e. a default of not using AI (P06 as a fallback rule, though P01 is not stated).
units.anchor: Students may use AI tools when course policies explicitly permit it
units.fit_note: Stated as permission when the course allows it, with the next sentence giving the silent-syllabus fallback.

units.why: 'When no policy is stated, only routine grammar corrections are allowed; any other AI use must be arranged with the instructor' is the rule when a syllabus is silent (P06).
units.anchor: When no policy is stated, only routine grammar corrections are allowed

units.why: 'Search features and autocomplete do not require arrangement or disclosure' exempts embedded features from the fallback (P07).
units.anchor: Search features and autocomplete do not require arrangement or disclosure
units.fit_note: An exemption for search and autocomplete rather than a rule on AI built into editors.

units.why: 'students are expected to be able to explain and defend any work they submit' requires understanding of all submitted work (P30).
units.anchor: students are expected to be able to explain and defend any work they submit

units.why: 'AI use exists on a spectrum from light assistance at one end to full content generation at the other' sets up levels of use that courses pick from (P05).
units.anchor: AI use exists on a spectrum from light assistance at one end to full content

units.why: 'AI embedded in tools you already use counts as GenAI use under this policy', including Copilot and Cursor assistants: a rule covering AI in IDEs (P07).
units.anchor: AI embedded in tools you already use counts as GenAI use under this policy

units.why: 'When a course restricts or requires disclosure of GenAI use, that applies to embedded tools as well as standalone ones' extends course rules to embedded AI (P07).
units.anchor: that applies to embedded tools as well as standalone ones

units.why: 'When you use AI on permitted work, disclose it at the point of submission' is a duty to disclose AI use with each submission (P24).
units.anchor: disclose it at the point of submission

units.why: The disclosure must 'identify the tool, the type of interaction, and what portion of the final work it contributed to', naming specific details (P25).
units.anchor: identify the tool, the type of interaction, and what portion of the final work

units.why: 'For agentic tools, describe the task given and the extent of its autonomy' sets disclosure details for agents (P25).
units.anchor: For agentic tools, describe the task given and the extent of its autonomy
units.fit_note: Adds agent-specific detail (task given and degree of autonomy), not tool, prompt or output.

units.why: 'A one-line disclosure is sufficient in most cases' limits how heavy the disclosure must be (P24).
units.anchor: A one-line disclosure is sufficient in most cases

units.why: Students are pointed to the OSU Library guidance for 'citing AI tools in APA, MLA, and Chicago formats', which is citation advice (P25).
units.anchor: guidance on citing AI tools in APA, MLA, and Chicago formats
units.fit_note: Refers to external citation formats rather than stating what a citation must contain.

units.why: 'Check with your instructor before using AI tools on sponsor-related deliverables' tells students to ask first where a sponsor may restrict AI (P10).
units.anchor: Check with your instructor before using AI tools on sponsor-related deliverables
units.fit_note: The trigger is external sponsor or industry-partner restrictions, not uncertainty about the course rule.

units.why: 'Do not upload a recording of a lecture, discussion, or any other person to an AI tool without the instructor's permission' bars uploading course recordings (P49).
units.anchor: Do not upload a recording of a lecture, discussion, or any other person to an

units.why: 'This section applies to research work by EECS graduate students, undergraduate researchers, and faculty' sets a research scope (P62).
units.anchor: This section applies to research work by EECS graduate students, undergraduate researchers, and faculty

units.why: 'Where venue, sponsor, IRB, or funder rules are stricter, those rules govern' defers to outside rules for research (P62).
units.anchor: Where venue, sponsor, IRB, or funder rules are stricter, those rules govern

units.why: 'The major advisor sets AI use norms for research conducted under their supervision' puts the research rule with the advisor (P62).
units.anchor: The major advisor sets AI use norms for research conducted under their supervision

units.why: Thesis expectations 'should be set with the full committee and documented early' is a research-specific planning step (P62).
units.anchor: AI use expectations should be set with the full committee and documented early

units.why: 'Where no norms have been set, AI tools may be used for grammar checking, search, and autocomplete without prior approval; any substantive use requires prior approval' is the research fallback (P62; P06 is course-syllabus fallback).
units.anchor: any substantive use requires prior approval

units.why: 'Blindly using or following AI output is itself an integrity concern' ties unverified AI use in research to integrity (P31).
units.anchor: Blindly using or following AI output is itself an integrity concern

units.why: 'The researcher is the author and accountable for the work' makes researchers own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: The researcher is the author and accountable for the work

units.why: 'Every factual claim, citation, quantitative result, and code path must be independently verified' because AI fabricates citations (P31).
units.anchor: Every factual claim, citation, quantitative result, and code path must be independently verified

units.why: 'AI-assisted text should be checked for similarity to existing work' recommends a similarity check (P40), here done by the researcher before submission.
units.anchor: AI-assisted text should be checked for similarity to existing work
units.fit_note: The researcher runs the similarity check on their own text; P40 is about staff identifying misuse.

units.why: 'The intellectual content ... must be the researcher's own' says the researcher owns the research question, design and analysis (P29).
units.anchor: must be the researcher's own

units.why: 'Researchers must be able to explain and justify any submitted text, analysis, or code' requires understanding of everything submitted (P30).
units.anchor: Researchers must be able to explain and justify any submitted text, analysis, or code

units.why: 'Where venue rules are silent, disclose substantive use in methods, acknowledgments' sets research disclosure (P24; P62 is about deferring to venues, not about disclosure).
units.anchor: Where venue rules are silent, disclose substantive use in methods, acknowledgments
units.fit_note: Research disclosure goes in methods or acknowledgments and names tool, task type and scope.

units.why: 'Do not upload sensitive or confidential material to nonapproved AI tools' protects confidential research data (P50).
units.anchor: Do not upload sensitive or confidential material to nonapproved AI tools

units.why: Prior published work 'cannot be reused verbatim in later documents even when the words are the researcher's own' and 'AI assistance does not change this': a copyright and ownership rule (P52).
units.anchor: cannot be reused verbatim in later documents even when the words are the researcher's own
units.policy: Prior work published under a copyright transfer (IEEE, ACM, Elsevier, Springer) cannot be reused verbatim in later documents even when the words are the researcher's own; AI assistance does not change this.
units.fit_note: Concerns self-plagiarism and copyright transfer, with AI making no difference.

units.why: 'It is recommended that students run a similarity check ... using Draft Coach' on documents for examination committees (P40).
units.anchor: It is recommended that students run a similarity check to other existing works
units.fit_note: A student-run similarity check before submission rather than staff detection.

units.why: 'Students should escalate disagreements to the Associate Head of Graduate Programs (AHGP)' names a route for disputes in research AI matters, which no type covers.
units.anchor: Students should escalate disagreements to the Associate Head of Graduate Programs (AHGP)
units.uncovered_note: Names who students escalate disagreements about research AI use to.

units.why: 'do not upload the document or its contents into non-approved AI tools for review assistance' sets a peer-review confidentiality rule (P62).
units.anchor: do not upload the document or its contents into non-approved AI tools for review assistance

units.why: 'Both NSF and NIH prohibit GenAI use in its peer review process' is a fact about funder rules for peer review (P62).
units.anchor: Both NSF and NIH prohibit GenAI use in its peer review process

units.why: 'The school of EECS expects every course syllabus to include an AI statement' is a school-level syllabus requirement (P09).
units.anchor: The school of EECS expects every course syllabus to include an AI statement

units.why: The CTL template has 'tiered icons and language covering the full range from prohibited to fully permitted use', pointing to named tiers (P05).
units.anchor: template with tiered icons and language covering the full range from prohibited to fully permitted

units.why: 'AI use permissions should align with course learning objectives so that grades reflect actual student mastery' ties AI rules to what is assessed (P35).
units.anchor: AI use permissions should align with course learning objectives

units.why: 'Learning outcome assessment should require independent demonstration of the underlying skill' favors assessment without AI help (P33).
units.anchor: Learning outcome assessment should require independent demonstration of the underlying skill
units.fit_note: Calls for independent demonstration without specifying proctoring or in-class formats.

units.why: 'Assignments that deviate from the course default, tighter or looser, should say so explicitly in the assignment prompt' sets how assignment-level exceptions are communicated (P09).
units.anchor: Assignments that deviate from the course default, tighter or looser, should say so explicitly
units.fit_note: Concerns assignment-level overrides of a course default.

units.why: 'Syllabi must not specify grade sanctions for academic misconduct; sanction determinations belong to the College Hearing Officer' forbids stating penalties, the opposite of P37, so it is left uncovered.
units.anchor: Syllabi must not specify grade sanctions for academic misconduct
units.uncovered_note: Syllabi may not state grade sanctions for misconduct because the College Hearing Officer decides sanctions.

units.why: Faculty 'can request a consultation with CTL' for drafting statements or designing AI-resilient assignments, which is faculty support (P63).
units.anchor: can request a consultation with CTL

units.why: 'Unauthorized AI use may constitute plagiarism, cheating, and / or falsification' classifies misuse as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Unauthorized AI use may constitute plagiarism, cheating, and / or falsification

units.why: Plagiarism is 'presenting AI-generated content as your own work without disclosure', a definition of misuse (P36).
units.anchor: presenting AI-generated content as your own work without disclosure

units.why: AI-generated text or code 'must be attributed in the work itself', marking AI-derived text or code where it is used (P27).
units.anchor: it must be attributed in the work itself

units.why: 'Submission-level disclosure does not substitute for in-text attribution' sets that a general statement is not enough, in addition to marking in place (P27).
units.anchor: Submission-level disclosure does not substitute for in-text attribution

units.why: Cheating is 'using AI to complete an assignment without prior authorization from your instructor', defining misuse as unauthorized use (P36).
units.anchor: using AI to complete an assignment without prior authorization from your instructor

units.why: Fabrication is 'using AI to create counterfeit citations, interview responses, or research results', a ban on deceptive and falsified AI use (P74).
units.anchor: using AI to create counterfeit citations, interview responses, or research results

units.why: Faculty 'should follow the formal reporting process' for AI-related violations, sending misuse through integrity channels (P36).
units.anchor: faculty should follow the formal reporting process outlined in Academic Integrity resources

units.why: 'AI detection tools are not reliable indicators of AI use' says detectors are unreliable (P39).
units.anchor: AI detection tools are not reliable indicators of AI use

units.why: Detectors 'cannot serve as sole evidence in a misconduct case', a limit on what proves misuse (P69).
units.anchor: cannot serve as sole evidence in a misconduct case
units.policy: AI detection tools cannot serve as sole evidence in a misconduct case.

units.why: 'A high AI probability score can encourage additional scrutiny but does not definitively prove' use says what a score may and may not support (P69).
units.anchor: A high AI probability score can encourage additional scrutiny but does not definitively prove

units.why: 'Faculty may not submit student work to AI detection tools that are not OSU Recommended and Approved' protects student data (P50).
units.anchor: Faculty may not submit student work to AI detection tools that are not OSU Recommended

units.why: 'A MOSS flag is not proof of AI use specifically, but it is legitimate evidence of potential misconduct' endorses code similarity tools as evidence (P40).
units.anchor: it is legitimate evidence of potential misconduct and may be submitted as part of a

units.why: 'Faculty should not conflate code similarity findings with AI detection findings' separates two kinds of evidence (P69).
units.anchor: Faculty should not conflate code similarity findings with AI detection findings

units.why: 'Faculty building a misconduct case should document behavioral evidence', listing kinds of evidence to weigh (P69).
units.anchor: Faculty building a misconduct case should document behavioral evidence

units.why: The categories are a spectrum 'across work products: text, code, simulations, circuit designs, lab reports', so they are named levels (P05).
units.anchor: The following categories define the spectrum of AI use

units.why: Clarification means 'using AI to explain difficult concepts, assignment prompts, or course material', a tutor-like use (P12).
units.anchor: using AI to explain difficult concepts, assignment prompts, or course material

units.why: Idea generation means 'brainstorming research topics, thesis statements, design concepts, or approaches' (P15).
units.anchor: brainstorming research topics, thesis statements, design concepts, or approaches

units.why: Summarization means 'condensing readings, lecture notes, or other materials to highlight key points', a study aid (P14).
units.anchor: condensing readings, lecture notes, or other materials to highlight key points

units.why: Translation is a prose-focused category: it 'does not include submitting AI-translated text as original work without disclosure' (P18).
units.anchor: using AI to translate assignment prompts, source materials, or your own drafted text into another

units.why: Editing, proofreading and formatting covers 'checking grammar, tone, punctuation, and clarity within your own drafted text' and not whole-paragraph rewrites (P18).
units.anchor: checking grammar, tone, punctuation, and clarity within your own drafted text

units.why: Coding assistance is 'debugging code you wrote, having AI explain an algorithm or concept, or generating sample code strictly for learning purposes', matching help with debugging (P13).
units.anchor: debugging code you wrote, having AI explain an algorithm or concept

units.why: Rewriting or refactoring means 'substantively rewriting portions of text or restructuring code you authored', a category for which no listed type fits.
units.anchor: substantively rewriting portions of text or restructuring code you authored
units.uncovered_note: Category of AI use: substantively rewriting text or refactoring code the student authored.

units.why: Analyzing data means 'using AI to generate conclusions or insights from a dataset', an analysis use not covered by a listed type.
units.anchor: using AI to generate conclusions or insights from a dataset
units.uncovered_note: Category of AI use: generating conclusions from datasets or running and interpreting simulation outputs.

units.why: The top category, an AI-generated work product, 'is prohibited unless explicitly permitted by the instructor', banning AI producing the submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: this is the highest-stakes category and is prohibited unless explicitly permitted by the instructor
units.policy: Using AI to produce the primary work submitted for an assignment, including text, code, graphics, audio, or other media, is prohibited unless explicitly permitted by the instructor, or unless the generated output is itself the object of analysis.

units.why: Mandatory disclosure covers uses such as 'Draft parts of the paper, significantly revise, or synthesize text', a tier of research disclosure (P24).
units.anchor: Draft parts of the paper, significantly revise, or synthesize text
units.policy: Disclosure of AI use in research is mandatory when using AI to formulate questions or hypotheses, design and conduct experiments, draft parts of the paper, significantly revise or synthesize text, translate, analyze or visualize data, extract data for a literature review, or generate synthetic data or figures.
units.fit_note: A tiered research table of what must, may, or need not be disclosed.

units.why: Optional disclosure covers 'Brainstorm or suggest how to organize a paper', lighter uses with no duty to disclose (P24).
units.anchor: Brainstorm or suggest how to organize a paper, or suggest a paper or section title
units.policy: Disclosure of AI use in research is optional when using AI to find references, find and generate examples for existing content, brainstorm or suggest how to organize a paper or title, or validate or give feedback on your own existing ideas, text, or code.
units.fit_note: The optional tier of a research disclosure table.

units.why: Disclosure is unnecessary for uses such as 'Check grammar, spelling, punctuation, or formatting within your own drafted text', the lowest tier (P24).
units.anchor: Check grammar, spelling, punctuation, or formatting within your own drafted text
units.policy: Disclosure of AI use in research is unnecessary when using AI to check grammar, spelling, punctuation or formatting of your own drafted text, search for sources, suggest clearer words, perform autocomplete, or act as a digital assistant.
units.fit_note: The no-disclosure tier of a research disclosure table.

documents.unit: School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), graduate programs (ECE, CS, AI)
documents.title: EECS Graduate Handbook 2025-2026, Section 2.21 Guidelines for AI writing assistance and proper citation and attribution
documents.summary: Section 2.21 of the EECS graduate handbook lets graduate students use AI tools only to polish and correct grammar in content they already created and bars AI-created new content or research. It recommends a similarity check (Draft Coach) and requires due diligence for documents going to examination committees.
documents.stance_why: The section says it is acceptable to use AI 'to polish and correct grammar of content already created' and that 'Students may not use AI tools to create new content or research.' Banned except for one narrow listed use, so restrict.

units.why: 'It is acceptable to use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) for writing assistance' only to polish and correct grammar of content already created: a narrow permitted prose use (P18).
units.anchor: It is acceptable to use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) for writing assistance

units.why: 'Students may not use AI tools to create new content or research' bans AI producing what students submit (P19).
units.anchor: Students may not use AI tools to create new content or research

units.why: 'The key issue is to ensure students are doing their own unique work and avoiding plagiarism issues' states that submitted work must be the student's own (P29).
units.anchor: students are doing their own unique work and avoiding plagiarism issues

units.why: 'Plagiarism is a serious offense with both short- and long-term consequences' presents plagiarism with AI as misconduct (P36), without stating concrete penalties.
units.anchor: Plagiarism is a serious offense with both short- and long-term consequences
units.fit_note: Treats plagiarism as serious but names no process or sanction.

units.why: AI tools 'may create content that is effectively copied from another author' warns that output can reproduce existing text and so carries a risk of unattributed copying (P31).
units.anchor: they may create content that is effectively copied from another author
units.fit_note: The risk is unattributed copying of existing writing, not factual error.

units.why: 'it is recommended that students use Draft Coach ... to check their work' for similarity with other works, especially if AI was involved (P40).
units.anchor: it is recommended that students use Draft Coach (available for free through OSU’s
units.fit_note: The student runs the check on their own work before submission.

units.why: The handbook explains that journals and societies such as IEEE acquire ownership of published text, so reusing it can trigger plagiarism checkers (P52).
units.anchor: the organization generally acquires ownership of the contents
units.policy: When a student publishes under a professional society such as IEEE, the organization generally acquires ownership of the contents through a copyright agreement, so re-used text can be flagged by a plagiarism checker even though the words are the student's own.
units.fit_note: Concerns self-plagiarism and copyright transfer rather than AI output.

units.why: 'It is the School's requirement that students perform due diligence ... for all documents submitted to their examination committees' makes the similarity check a duty before submission (P40).
units.anchor: It is the School’s requirement that students perform due diligence
units.fit_note: Required similarity check by the student, not staff detection.

units.why: Students with questions on 'proper policy, attribution, or academic integrity' should 'check with their major advisor and/or with the AHGP' (P10).
units.anchor: check with their major advisor and/or with the AHGP
